questions.text: In MVI, a reducer receives an intent that requires fetching data from the network. What should it do?
options: Call the repository and return state with the result
Return unchanged state or a loading flag — the store/ViewModel layer starts the I/O
Start a coroutine and update state in the callback
Throw an exception, because reducers do not handle such intents
questions.explanation: A reducer must remain a pure function, (State, Intent) -> State. Doing I/O inside it destroys determinism, makes tests require mocks, and breaks time travel because replaying state would repeat the network request. Side effects are started by the store after reduction, and their results return as separate Internal intents.

questions.text: Why should one-off events (snackbar, navigation) not be fields in State?
options: Because they increase the size of the state object
Because State is replayable — after recomposition or rotation the event would run again
Because Compose cannot render events
Because StateFlow does not support nullable types
questions.explanation: State describes what is TRUE at a given moment and is replayed on every recomposition and after configuration changes. An event stored in state would be consumed multiple times. Use a Channel with receiveAsFlow for exactly one receiver, or a SharedFlow with explicit acknowledgement.

questions.text: A MutableSharedFlow without replay was chosen to store one-off effects. What bug will appear?
options: Effects will be duplicated after screen rotation
An effect sent before the collector attaches will be lost forever
Effects will be delivered in random order
No bug will appear — it is equivalent to Channel
questions.explanation: SharedFlow without replay is hot and does not buffer for absent subscribers. If a network error happens while the screen is being recreated, the snackbar will never appear. Channel buffers the event until it is received, so it is the right choice for effects targeted at a single receiver.
questions.code:
private val _effects = MutableSharedFlow<Effect>()   // drops events
private val _effects = Channel<Effect>(Channel.BUFFERED)  // does not drop them

questions.text: Optimistic update: the user taps a star, saving is in progress, then taps again. Where is the best place to protect against the double tap?
options: Set enabled = false on the button in Compose
Debounce clicks in the ViewModel
In the reducer — if the id is in savingFavorites, return state unchanged
With an isLoading flag in the ViewModel outside state
questions.explanation: Putting the guard in the reducer is testable without UI and works no matter how many views dispatch intents. enabled=false is only presentation-layer protection and does not stop programmatic dispatch or a race. The store can also detect no state change (before == after) and skip I/O.

questions.text: How do Intent.Ui and Intent.Internal differ, and why make that split?
options: Ui intents are synchronous, Internal intents are asynchronous
Ui expresses a user intention, Internal describes a fact that already happened (an I/O result)
Internal intents are private and do not go through the reducer
It is only a naming convention with no technical meaning
questions.explanation: Ui intents are requests or wishes, such as QueryChanged; Internal intents are past-tense facts, such as LoadSucceeded. Both go through the same reducer, so EVERY state change has a name and appears on the timeline. Without the split, I/O results would set state directly and create a second hidden mutation path.

questions.text: In MviStore, intents go into a Channel consumed by a single loop. What does that guarantee?
options: That intents cannot be lost under load
Serialized reduction — two parallel dispatches cannot interleave state reads and writes
That reduction runs on Dispatchers.Main
Automatic deduplication of duplicate intents
questions.explanation: A single consumer ensures reduce() never runs concurrently. The reducer therefore needs no locks, and middleware observes consistent before/after pairs. See the MVI Loop scenario in the Sync tab: 100 parallel dispatches and zero lost intents.

questions.text: A screen has isLoading, error, and users fields. Where should showEmptyState be placed?
options: As a separate Boolean field in State, set by the reducer
As a computed property (get()) in the State class
In the Composable function, just before rendering the list
In the ViewModel as a separate StateFlow
questions.explanation: Derived state computed in State is a single source of truth, testable without UI, and impossible to forget in one of several rendering places. A separate Boolean field would have to be updated in every reducer branch and would eventually drift from the rest of the state.

questions.text: Time travel debugging is possible in MVI, but not in typical MVVM. Why?
options: Because MVI uses immutable data structures
Because every state change goes through one named function, so the (intent, state) history fully describes the session
Because StateFlow stores the history of values
Because Compose saves recomposition snapshots
questions.explanation: The key is not immutability alone, but the existence of exactly ONE place where state transitions happen. In MVVM, scattered methods mutate state, so a complete ordered list of transitions cannot be collected or replayed.

questions.text: A form has 30 fields. You create 30 separate FieldXChanged intents. What is the problem?
options: Performance — too many intent objects
Excess boilerplate; one Intent with a form model or field reference is better
The reducer cannot handle that many when branches
There is no problem — this is correct MVI usage
questions.explanation: MVI is not a dogma. For large forms, 30 intents and 30 when branches are pure cost without benefit. A more reasonable approach is FieldChanged(field: FormField, value: String) or FormUpdated(form: FormModel). The pattern should serve readability, not the other way around.

questions.text: The store performs I/O in onIntentProcessed. Why should this method NOT be suspend and block the loop?
options: Because suspend does not work in abstract classes
Because a long-running task would block processing of subsequent intents and freeze the whole screen
Because it would violate reducer purity
Because Channel does not support suspend functions
questions.explanation: The intent loop must remain responsive. If it waited for a network request to finish, the user could not even collapse a panel or type the next letter. Side effects should be launched in separate coroutines, and their results should come back as intents.

questions.text: What is the expect/actual mechanism used for?
options: Declaring optional dependencies in Gradle
Declaring an API in common code and providing an implementation per platform
Marking code that requires opt-in
Generating Objective-C headers
questions.explanation: expect declares a contract in commonMain, while actual provides implementations in androidMain or iosMain. Note that this is not always the best solution: often a plain interface in commonMain plus DI-provided implementations is cleaner because it is easier to test and replace.

questions.text: Kotlin/Native has used the new memory model since version 1.7.20. What changed?
options: The garbage collector disappeared
Object freezing and the restriction on sharing state between threads disappeared
Objects are always copied between threads
Kotlin/Native switched to reference counting like Swift
questions.explanation: The old model required freeze() and threw InvalidMutabilityException when mutating a shared object, which was the biggest KMP barrier. The new model allows state to be shared between threads much like on the JVM, so coroutines and Flow work on Kotlin/Native without workarounds.

questions.text: How can you expose Flow from common code to Swift in a convenient way for iOS?
options: Directly — Swift natively understands Flow
Wrap it in your own callback/AsyncSequence wrapper or use SKIE/KMP-NativeCoroutines
Convert Flow to LiveData
Export only suspend functions; Flow cannot be exposed
questions.explanation: Kotlin/Native exports suspend functions as functions with completion handlers, but Flow has no direct Swift equivalent. Solutions include a custom wrapper with subscription and a cancellation handle, or tools such as SKIE and KMP-NativeCoroutines that generate native AsyncSequence APIs.

questions.text: Which application layers are most valuable to share in KMP?
options: Only the UI layer
Domain and data (models, use cases, repositories), with UI optionally shared through Compose Multiplatform
Only data models
All or nothing — KMP does not allow partial sharing
questions.explanation: The biggest gain comes from sharing business logic and the data layer, where complexity and costly bugs usually live. UI can be shared with Compose Multiplatform, but that is an independent decision: many teams keep native UI, such as SwiftUI, while sharing only domain logic. KMP allows any degree of sharing.

questions.text: How does the commonMain source set differ from androidMain and iosMain?
options: commonMain compiles only for Android
commonMain contains code for all targets and has no access to platform APIs
androidMain takes precedence over commonMain in name conflicts
iosMain is generated automatically from commonMain
questions.explanation: commonMain is compiled for every target, so it can use only APIs available everywhere, such as the standard library and kotlinx libraries. Platform code belongs in androidMain or iosMain, which see commonMain and can provide actual implementations. The hierarchy can be extended with intermediate source sets, such as nativeMain or appleMain.

questions.text: In commonMain you need to read a file from resources. Which approach is compatible with KMP?
options: java.io.File — it works on both platforms
Compose Multiplatform Resources (Res.readBytes) or a custom interface with implementations per platform
An android.content.Context passed into commonMain
kotlin.io.readLine with redirection
questions.explanation: java.io.File and Context are JVM/Android APIs, unavailable in commonMain. Compose Resources provides shared Res.readBytes working on both platforms. Another option is your own port, such as a Source interface with actual implementations, which also improves testability; this project does exactly that with LessonsSource.

questions.text: The following code run by 100 coroutines on ONE thread produces a result smaller than 100. Why?
options: Because Dispatchers.Default uses multiple cores
Because yield() creates a suspension point between the read and the write, where other coroutines can enter
Because the var is not marked @Volatile
Because async does not guarantee all tasks will run
questions.explanation: This is the key coroutine intuition: concurrency is not parallelism. A race appears anywhere a suspension point sits between a read and a write, even on one thread. @Volatile does not help because the issue is not memory visibility, but atomicity of the read-modify-write operation.
questions.code:
var counter = 0
List(100) { async { val read = counter; yield(); counter = read + 1 } }.awaitAll()

questions.text: What is wrong with this catch block?
options: Nothing — this is correct error handling
It swallows CancellationException, so the parent treats the cancelled coroutine as completed successfully
It should catch Throwable instead of Exception
It is missing a finally block
questions.explanation: CancellationException is a control signal for structured concurrency, not a domain error. Swallowing it breaks cancellation propagation: the scope thinks the child finished normally. Always rethrow it, for example catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }, before a general catch.

questions.text: When does async { }.await() called immediately on the next line make sense?
options: Always — async is faster than a normal call
Practically never; it parallelizes nothing, adds overhead, and changes exception propagation
When you want to run code on another dispatcher
When the function is not marked suspend
questions.explanation: async is useful only when you start several tasks and then wait for all of them. async { X }.await() is a complicated way to write X(), with additional exception wrapping. Use withContext to change dispatchers.

questions.text: A repository suspend function performs a network request. Who is responsible for switching to Dispatchers.IO?
options: The ViewModel — it should call it in launch(Dispatchers.IO)
The function itself, using withContext(Dispatchers.IO) internally, so it is safe to call from Main
Nobody — coroutines choose the correct thread automatically
The DI layer, by injecting the dispatcher into the ViewModel
questions.explanation: Main-safety means a suspend function must be safe to call from any dispatcher, including Main. Forcing callers to know the implementation detail that something is I/O breaks encapsulation; if the repository later changes to an in-memory cache, all those calls would be wrong.

questions.text: How does collectLatest differ from collect when processing search requests?
options: collectLatest skips values, collect processes all of them
collectLatest cancels processing of the previous value when a new one appears
collectLatest is asynchronous, collect blocks
collectLatest deduplicates identical values
questions.explanation: collectLatest does not skip values; it starts the block for each one, but cancels the previous execution if it is still running. This prevents the classic search bug where a slower response for an old query overwrites fresher results. The operator equivalent is flatMapLatest.

questions.text: How does MutableStateFlow.update { } differ from assigning .value = ?
options: update is faster because it skips notifying subscribers
update performs the operation in a compare-and-set loop, so it is atomic; .value = is a plain write
update works only inside a coroutine
There is no difference — update is an alias for .value =
questions.explanation: The read-modify-write pattern on .value is race-prone just like a regular field. update repeats the lambda until the write succeeds, so the lambda must be pure and fast because it may run more than once. See the StateFlow scenarios in the Sync tab.

questions.text: A while (true) { heavyComputation() } loop in a coroutine does not react to cancellation. Why?
options: Because cancellation works only on Dispatchers.IO
Because cancellation is cooperative — code must check isActive or call a suspend function
Because the while loop blocks the parent Job
Because the @Cancellable annotation is missing
questions.explanation: Coroutines cannot be killed from the outside. Cancellation sets a flag that the code must check itself; kotlinx.coroutines suspend functions, ensureActive(), isActive, and yield() do that. A purely computational loop without those calls will run to completion despite scope cancellation.

questions.text: What is SupervisorJob for, and how does it differ from a regular Job?
options: It automatically retries failed tasks
Failure of one child does not cancel sibling children or the parent
It allows launching coroutines without a scope
It guarantees execution on the main thread
questions.explanation: With a regular Job, a child failure cancels the parent, which then cancels the remaining children. SupervisorJob isolates failures; viewModelScope uses it so one failed request does not kill the whole screen. Note that supervisorScope applies only to direct children.

questions.text: A runTest test with StandardTestDispatcher does not see an event sent to a Channel, even after advanceUntilIdle(). What is the most common cause?
options: The Channel was closed before receiving
The collector in backgroundScope starts lazily; UnconfinedTestDispatcher is needed so it receives immediately
runTest does not support channels
advanceUntilIdle does not work with Channel.BUFFERED
questions.explanation: With StandardTestDispatcher, when the collector starts depends on task ordering in the queue, making the test nondeterministic. Starting the collector with UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler) makes it start immediately and receive the event at send time. This exact issue occurred in this project’s tests.

questions.text: How does Flow (cold) differ from StateFlow (hot)?
options: Flow runs on IO, StateFlow on Main
Flow executes from scratch for every collector and has no value; StateFlow always has a value and is shared
StateFlow does not support map and filter operators
Flow requires a coroutine, StateFlow does not
questions.explanation: A cold Flow is a recipe: each collect runs it separately. StateFlow is a hot value holder: it has an initial value, deduplicates consecutive equal values with built-in distinctUntilChanged semantics, and shares the same value among subscribers. That is why StateFlow fits screen state, while plain Flow fits one-shot queries.

questions.text: Why is GlobalScope discouraged?
options: Because it does not support Dispatchers.Main
Because the coroutine has no parent — nobody cancels it, leading to leaks and work after the screen closes
Because it is slower than viewModelScope
Because it works only in tests
questions.explanation: GlobalScope is like new Thread() without keeping a reference: nothing cancels it, so the coroutine can outlive the screen or even the whole user session. It breaks structured concurrency. If work must truly outlive the screen, use an application-scoped CoroutineScope with an explicit lifecycle or WorkManager.

questions.text: What does flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) do, and what does it affect?
options: It changes the dispatcher of the collector (the collect block)
It changes the dispatcher of operators ABOVE it in the chain, and does not affect collect
It moves the whole chain, including collect, to IO
It is equivalent to withContext(Dispatchers.IO)
questions.explanation: flowOn works upstream in the chain: it affects emission and operators defined before it. The collect block always runs in the caller’s context. This is intentional: collect in the ViewModel remains on Main and can safely update state.

questions.text: What is the coroutine-world equivalent of RxJava Single<T>?
options: Flow<T>
suspend fun (): T
StateFlow<T>
Deferred<T> created by GlobalScope.async
questions.explanation: Single emits exactly one value or an error, which is precisely the semantics of a suspend function returning T. Maybe<T> maps to suspend fun (): T?, and Completable maps to suspend fun (): Unit. Flow corresponds to Observable/Flowable, streams of many values.

questions.text: Which Rx operator corresponds to Flow flatMapLatest?
options: flatMap
concatMap
switchMap
combineLatest
questions.explanation: switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner stream when a new value arrives, exactly like flatMapLatest. flatMap corresponds to flatMapMerge, running concurrently without cancellation, while concatMap is flatMapConcat, sequential with queuing.

questions.text: What is the main reason Flow replaced RxJava in new Android projects?
options: Flow has more operators
Structured concurrency — cancellation is inherited from the scope, without manually managing Disposable
Flow is faster in benchmarks
RxJava does not support backpressure
questions.explanation: In Rx, every subscription must be remembered and disposed, for example CompositeDisposable.clear(); forgetting dispose is a classic leak. In coroutines, cancellation follows the scope structure. Flow also works in Kotlin Multiplatform, while RxJava is a JVM library. Rx still has richer operators and stronger backpressure support.

questions.text: The Kotlin equivalent of BehaviorSubject<T> is:
options: MutableSharedFlow<T>()
MutableStateFlow<T>(initial)
Channel<T>(CONFLATED)
callbackFlow { }
questions.explanation: BehaviorSubject stores the latest value and delivers it to new subscribers, which is StateFlow semantics. PublishSubject, which has only new values and no history, corresponds to MutableSharedFlow without replay. StateFlow differs by requiring an initial value and deduplicating equal values.

questions.text: You are migrating Single<List<User>> from a legacy repository to a coroutine-based ViewModel. What is the simplest approach?
options: Rewrite the whole repository to coroutines before migrating the ViewModel
Use the kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 bridge: single.await()
Manually wrap the subscription in suspendCancellableCoroutine
Block the thread with single.blockingGet()
questions.explanation: kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 provides ready-made bridges in both directions: await() for Single/Maybe, asFlow() for Observable, and asObservable() back. It lets you migrate gradually from presentation downward. blockingGet() blocks a thread and defeats the point of coroutines, while manual suspendCancellableCoroutine duplicates existing code.

questions.text: How do subscribeOn and observeOn differ in RxJava?
options: subscribeOn affects emission (the source), observeOn switches the thread for operators below it
subscribeOn affects receiving, observeOn affects emission
Both do the same thing; observeOn is deprecated
subscribeOn works once, observeOn only in Flowable
questions.explanation: subscribeOn chooses the thread on which the source starts, and only the first call in the chain matters. observeOn switches the thread for everything after it and can appear multiple times. In coroutines this split disappears: flowOn works upstream, while collect always runs in the caller’s context.

questions.text: What does RxJava have more of than Flow?
options: Kotlin Multiplatform support
Backpressure as a first-class concept (Flowable with strategies) and richer time-based operators
Compose integration
Type safety
questions.explanation: Flowable has explicit backpressure strategies such as BUFFER, DROP, and LATEST, and Rx offers mature time operators: window, throttleFirst, sample, debounce in many variants. In Flow, some of this is assembled manually with buffer(), conflate(), and sample(). In typical mobile apps it is rarely needed.

questions.text: A class reads a file, parses JSON, and caches the result. Which principle does it violate, and how should it be fixed?
options: Open/Closed — add a base interface
Single Responsibility — split it into a source, a parser, and a repository that wires them together
Liskov Substitution — extract a base class
It violates none — “providing data” is one cohesive responsibility
questions.explanation: It has three reasons to change: the data format, the source, and the cache policy. Splitting it into LessonsSource (where from), LessonsJsonParser (how to understand it), and LessonJsonRepository (wiring plus cache) lets the parser be tested without Android and the source be replaced by network without touching parsing.

questions.text: A UserRepository interface has getUsers, setFavorite, exportCsv, syncWithCloud, and clearCache. Which principle does that violate?
options: Dependency Inversion
Interface Segregation
Liskov Substitution
Open/Closed
questions.explanation: Interface Segregation says a client should not depend on methods it does not use. The list screen needs two methods, but a test fake must implement five. The fix is several narrow interfaces, possibly implemented by one class, like UserRepository plus NetworkFailureSwitch in this project.

questions.text: An implementation of an interface throws UnsupportedOperationException in one method. Which principle is broken?
options: Single Responsibility
Liskov Substitution
Interface Segregation
Open/Closed
questions.explanation: LSP says a subtype must be usable wherever the base type is expected, without surprises. Throwing an exception forces clients to check the concrete type, such as if (repo is ReadOnly), defeating the abstraction. It is usually also a signal that ISP is broken: the interface is too broad.

questions.text: A sealed interface forces every when to be updated after adding a new subtype. Does that violate Open/Closed?
options: Yes — we modify existing code instead of extending it
It is a deliberate trade-off: we lose some OCP and gain compiler-checked exhaustiveness
No, because when is not part of the class
Yes, so sealed should be replaced with open inheritance
questions.explanation: This is a real trade-off, not blind rule following. An open hierarchy fits OCP better, but allows a silent runtime bug when a new type is forgotten. sealed turns that into a compile error; for finite sets such as states, content blocks, or intents, that is usually the better choice.

questions.text: A project has domain/, data/, and presentation/ folders, but the ViewModel imports a Retrofit API class. What does that mean?
options: Nothing bad, if the import is in one place
This is not Clean Architecture — dependency direction matters, not folder structure
It violates Open/Closed
It is only an aesthetic problem
questions.explanation: Folders are a convention; architecture is defined by the dependency graph. A ViewModel that knows Retrofit means presentation depends directly on an infrastructure detail. Tests then need a server or HTTP mocks, and changing the networking library touches the presentation layer.
