questions.text: Which symptom most often reveals a Dependency Inversion violation?
options: The class has more than 200 lines
A unit test requires the network, a database, or an Android Context
The interface has more than 5 methods
A method accepts more than 3 parameters
questions.explanation: If high-level logic depends directly on infrastructure details, it cannot be isolated in a test. Needing an emulator, a server, or a database to test a business rule is the most practical indicator that DIP has been violated.

questions.text: How does remember { } differ from rememberSaveable { }?
options: rememberSaveable works only with primitive types
remember survives recomposition; rememberSaveable also survives configuration changes and process death
remember is faster because it does not serialize
There is no difference except the name
questions.explanation: remember caches a value across recompositions, but it is lost on screen rotation. rememberSaveable stores it in a Bundle through a Saver, so it survives configuration changes and process death. In MVI, both are rarely needed for screen state because that state lives in the ViewModel.

questions.text: A LazyColumn list without a key parameter behaves strangely when an item is removed from the middle. Why?
options: Because LazyColumn requires key to work
Without a stable key, Compose identifies items by position, so state and animations get assigned to the wrong items
Because missing key disables view recycling
Because a key is needed only for animations
questions.explanation: By default, an item’s identity is its index. After removing an item from the middle, all following items “shift”, so state remembered per item, such as expansion, scroll, or animation, moves to the wrong row. key = { it.id } binds state to data identity, not position.

questions.text: When is using derivedStateOf justified?
options: Always when computing a value derived from state
When frequently changing state produces a value that changes rarely, limiting recompositions
To store state that survives screen rotation
For background computations off the main thread
questions.explanation: The classic example is listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 for an “up” button. Scroll changes every frame, but the boolean result changes rarely, so derivedStateOf limits recompositions to actual result changes. For cheap computations from rarely changing sources, it is unnecessary overhead.

questions.text: How should one-off effects from a ViewModel be collected in a Composable?
options: In an init block of the Composable function
In LaunchedEffect with a key stable with respect to the ViewModel instance
In remember { }
Using collectAsState()
questions.explanation: LaunchedEffect starts a coroutine tied to the composition lifecycle and cancels it when leaving; when the key changes, it restarts. The key should be a stable reference such as viewModel, not mutable state, otherwise the collector would restart on every state change and lose events. collectAsState is for state, not events.

questions.text: What is type stability (@Stable/@Immutable) in Compose and why does it matter?
options: It guarantees thread safety for the type
It lets Compose skip recomposition when parameters have not changed
It forces the use of data class
It enables automatic memoization of function results
questions.explanation: Compose can skip recomposition if all parameters are stable and equal to their previous values. An unstable type, such as a java.util List instead of kotlinx ImmutableList or a class with var, forces recomposition every time. That is why MVI State should hold immutable structures.

questions.text: Which way of passing state to a component makes golden tests and previews easier?
options: Injecting the ViewModel into every component
State hoisting — the component takes state and event lambdas as parameters
Using CompositionLocal for screen state
A global state object
questions.explanation: A stateless component that accepts (state, onIntent) can be rendered with any state, including an error state, without starting the ViewModel or the whole app. This makes golden tests trivial: pass a prepared State and compare the bitmap. In MVI this pattern emerges naturally.

questions.text: What exactly does “smoke test” mean?
options: A performance test under load
A test role: a narrow set of checks that the build is not fundamentally broken
A UI rendering test to a bitmap
A test run only on a device
questions.explanation: A smoke test is a role, not a technology. It answers whether it is worth running the rest of the tests at all: whether the DI graph builds, the start screen renders, and the main path works. It can be a unit or UI test; scope and timing define it.

questions.text: What are golden (screenshot) tests, and what do they catch better than UI tests?
options: They check rendering performance
They render a component and compare it with an approved baseline, catching visual regressions such as padding, colors, and clipped text
They test business logic from state snapshots
They verify accessibility
questions.explanation: An assertion like onNodeWithText("Anna").assertIsDisplayed() also passes when the text is white on a white background or clipped off-screen. A golden test compares pixels. Tools include Paparazzi and Roborazzi on the JVM without an emulator, Compose Preview Screenshot Testing, and swift-snapshot-testing on iOS.

questions.text: Why does MVI work especially well with golden tests?
options: Because MVI forces the use of Compose
Because any State can be passed directly and rendered without going through interactions
Because State is automatically serialized to a file
Because the reducer generates screenshots
questions.explanation: To photograph an error state in MVVM, you usually have to simulate a network failure and click through the path. In MVI, UsersState(error = "HTTP 503") and render is enough. Every state variant becomes a one-line test case.

questions.text: In a KMP project you have a reducer in commonMain. Where should its logic be tested?
options: Separately in Kotlin tests and in XCTest in Xcode
Once in commonTest — the same tests run on the JVM and on the iOS simulator
Only in androidHostTest
In instrumentation tests on both platforms
questions.explanation: Tests in commonTest compile for every target: ./gradlew :shared:testAndroidHostTest and :shared:iosSimulatorArm64Test run the same code. Duplicating these tests in Swift doubles maintenance with no gain; keep only truly iOS-specific tests in Xcode, such as the Swift layer and XCUITest.

questions.text: A ViewModel test with a 350 ms debounce and 700 ms network delay runs in milliseconds. How?
options: By reducing delays in test configuration
runTest with TestDispatcher uses virtual time — advanceTimeBy moves the clock without real waiting
By running tests in parallel
By replacing delay with Thread.sleep(0)
questions.explanation: TestScheduler virtualizes time: delay(700) completes immediately after advanceUntilIdle(). This lets you test real timeouts and debounce without slowing the build. Changing constants for tests would mean testing different code than production.

questions.text: You are writing a test scenario that demonstrates a race condition. How do you make it repeatable?
options: Run the test 1000 times and check whether it failed at least once
Force the interleaving with an explicit suspension point, yield, between the read and the write
Use Thread.sleep with a random duration
Mark the test as @Flaky and ignore instability
questions.explanation: A test that depends on accidental interleaving is unstable and worthless; sometimes it passes despite the bug. Inserting yield() at the critical point makes the race deterministic. That is how the Sync tab scenarios work: they always lose writes on every platform.

questions.text: You are testing a ViewModel that uses Dispatchers.Main. What should be done in setUp?
options: Nothing — Dispatchers.Main works in JVM tests
Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher), and Dispatchers.resetMain() in tearDown
Replace viewModelScope with your own CoroutineScope
Run the test on Robolectric
questions.explanation: Dispatchers.Main requires an Android Looper, which JVM tests do not have; without replacement you get ModuleNotFound or IllegalStateException. Dispatchers.setMain from kotlinx-coroutines-test installs a TestDispatcher so viewModelScope uses virtual time. resetMain prevents state leaking between tests.

questions.text: Why test the DI dependency graph?
options: To measure app startup time
Because a missing definition appears only at runtime; the test turns it into a build failure
Because Koin requires tests to work
To generate module documentation
questions.explanation: Koin resolves dependencies lazily, so a missing definition appears only when a screen is first opened, possibly by a user. A simple test calling koin.get() for key types moves that failure to CI. The DI graph is code too, and it breaks too.

questions.text: Middleware in MviStore observes reductions. Why is it deliberately NOT allowed to change state?
options: Because it runs on another thread
Because it would create a second hidden mutation point beside the reducer
Because middleware is called before reduction
Because it has no access to the State object
questions.explanation: The entire value of MVI relies on exactly one place where state transitions happen. Middleware that can mutate state would turn a predictable chain into a system where state changes in places invisible on the timeline. Logging, analytics, and crash reporting do not require mutation.

questions.text: A reducer returns the same state object (before == after). How can the store use that?
options: Skip notifying subscribers and do not start the side effect
Automatically retry the intent
Remove the entry from the timeline
Report an error — a reducer should always return a new object
questions.explanation: StateFlow already deduplicates equal values, so the UI will not refresh unnecessarily. In addition, the store can infer that the intent was ignored, for example a tap during saving, and skip I/O. UsersViewModel uses exactly this pattern for FavoriteToggled.

questions.text: A detail screen reads data from the same ViewModel as the list. What is the main advantage?
options: Memory savings
No data duplication — the star in the list and details cannot diverge
Faster navigation
Ability to use the same reducer
questions.explanation: Two independent sources of the same data sooner or later fall out of sync, because every change must be propagated. One source of truth eliminates that entire class of bugs. The trade-off is coupling between screens, so independent features are better served by separate stores.

questions.text: A store has a list of 10,000 items. The reducer does state.copy(users = ...) on every intent. Is that a problem?
options: Yes, copy copies the whole list, so mutable state is needed
No, copy creates a new state object, but references to unchanged collections are shared
Yes, therefore MVI is unsuitable for large lists
No, because Kotlin optimizes copy into in-place mutation
questions.explanation: data class copy() is shallow: it copies references, not collection contents. The cost is proportional to the number of fields, not the amount of data. Real cost appears only when the list is actually transformed with map or filter, and that is independent of the architectural pattern.

questions.text: How does coroutineScope { } differ from supervisorScope { }?
options: coroutineScope runs on Main, supervisorScope on Default
In coroutineScope, a child failure cancels siblings; in supervisorScope, children are isolated
supervisorScope does not wait for children to finish
coroutineScope cannot contain async
questions.explanation: Both wait for all children to complete, but they differ in error propagation. Use coroutineScope when all tasks are required and a missing one makes the result useless. Use supervisorScope when tasks are independent and a partial result still has value.

questions.text: What does the buffer() operator do in Flow?
options: Groups values into lists of a specified size
Lets the producer continue emitting while the consumer is still processing, separating them with a buffer
Writes values to a disk cache
Delays emission by a specified time
questions.explanation: By default, Flow is sequential: emission waits for collect to finish. buffer() introduces a channel between them, so production and consumption run concurrently, useful when both stages are costly. Variants include conflate(), which keeps only the latest value, and collectLatest, which cancels processing.

questions.text: When is withContext(Dispatchers.Main) in a ViewModel unnecessary?
options: Always — a ViewModel should not touch Main
When using viewModelScope, which runs on Dispatchers.Main.immediate by default
When updating StateFlow
When the function is marked suspend
questions.explanation: viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate by default, so the code is already running on the main thread. An extra withContext(Main) is unnecessary overhead. It is also worth knowing that updating StateFlow is thread-safe and does not require Main.

questions.text: What happens when an unhandled exception is thrown inside launch { } in viewModelScope?
options: It is silently ignored
It goes to CoroutineExceptionHandler, and without one it crashes the app
It is retried automatically
It cancels all other coroutines in viewModelScope
questions.explanation: launch propagates exceptions up the hierarchy; without a handler, they reach the platform default handler and the app crashes. viewModelScope uses SupervisorJob, so it does not cancel siblings, but the exception still must be handled. In async, the exception is stored and thrown only at await().

questions.text: How does Channel.CONFLATED differ from Channel.BUFFERED?
options: CONFLATED drops new values when the buffer is full; BUFFERED suspends
CONFLATED stores only the latest value, overwriting the previous one
CONFLATED works only with one receiver
There is no difference for a single consumer
questions.explanation: CONFLATED, capacity one with overwriting, is appropriate when only the freshest state matters, such as scroll position. It would be a bug for one-off effects: two messages sent quickly would lose the first one. That is why effects should use BUFFERED or UNLIMITED.

questions.text: What is callbackFlow used for?
options: Converting Flow to a callback
Wrapping callback-based APIs into Flow, with cancellation handled by awaitClose
Running Flow in the background
Combining many Flows into one
questions.explanation: callbackFlow turns classic APIs such as listeners, BroadcastReceiver, or LocationManager into a stream. The key is awaitClose { }, where you unregister the listener on cancellation. Without it, you leak resources; the compiler even enforces its presence.

questions.text: Why can code in commonMain not use java.time.LocalDate?
options: Because that API is deprecated
Because it is a JVM class, and commonMain must also compile for Kotlin/Native
Because it requires minSdk 26
Because Kotlin has its own type with that name
questions.explanation: commonMain can use only APIs available to all targets: the Kotlin standard library and multiplatform libraries. For dates use kotlinx-datetime, for serialization kotlinx-serialization, and for I/O okio or ktor. Alternatively use expect/actual or an interface with per-platform implementations.

questions.text: An iOS framework generated from a KMP module exports a Kotlin class with a sealed interface. How does it look in Swift?
options: As a Swift enum with associated values
As a protocol with implementing classes, without exhaustive switch matching
As a struct with a type field
It is not exported
questions.explanation: Kotlin sealed has no equivalent in Objective-C, which the interop goes through. In Swift you get a protocol and classes, and switch requires a default branch because the compiler cannot check exhaustiveness. Tools such as SKIE generate native Swift enums and restore exhaustive matching.

questions.text: Which approach is better for injecting platform dependencies in KMP?
options: Always expect/actual
An interface in commonMain plus a per-platform implementation injected by DI
A static singleton initialized in Application
Reflection
questions.explanation: expect/actual is convenient for small things such as a platform name or UUID generator, but it is hard to test and replace because you cannot fake an actual. An interface in commonMain with implementations registered in per-platform DI modules gives full testability and follows DIP.

questions.text: How does Observable differ from Flowable in RxJava?
options: Observable is synchronous, Flowable is asynchronous
Flowable supports backpressure; Observable does not
Observable emits one value, Flowable many
Flowable is deprecated
questions.explanation: Flowable implements Reactive Streams and lets the consumer signal how many values it can accept with request(n), using strategies such as BUFFER, DROP, and LATEST. Observable emits without limits, which can cause OutOfMemoryError with a fast producer and slow consumer. Flow solves this differently, by suspending the emitter.

questions.text: This code has a memory leak. Where?
options: In the map operator
The subscription is not stored anywhere or disposed when the screen is destroyed
In using Schedulers.io()
There is no leak
questions.explanation: subscribe() returns a Disposable that must be kept and disposed, for example CompositeDisposable.clear() in onDestroy or onCleared. Without that, the subscription continues to live and holds a reference to the view. Structured concurrency is exactly what removed this class of bugs in coroutines.

questions.text: The Flow equivalent of Rx doOnNext is:
options: onStart
onEach
onCompletion
transform
questions.explanation: onEach performs a side effect for every value while passing the value downstream, exactly like doOnNext. Related operators are onStart, similar to doOnSubscribe; onCompletion, similar to doFinally and also called on error and cancellation; and catch, similar to onErrorResumeNext.

questions.text: A repository returns Result<List<User>> instead of throwing an exception. What is the advantage?
options: Better performance
The error is part of the signature, so the compiler forces handling it
It enables use in commonMain
Automatic retry of requests
questions.explanation: The Result type makes the error path visible in the API, so it is harder to miss than an undocumented exception. The cost is more ceremony at each call site. Beware the trap: Result can also catch CancellationException, so coroutine code must explicitly rethrow cancellation.

questions.text: Which elements should NEVER appear in the domain layer?
options: Repository interfaces
@Serializable, @Entity annotations, Retrofit types, and Android classes
Domain exception classes
Business models
questions.explanation: The domain must be independent of frameworks; otherwise changing the serialization or database library forces changes in business rules, and tests cannot run without those libraries. In KMP there is an even stricter limit: Android classes in domain would prevent iOS compilation.

questions.text: DTO → domain model mapping should be located in:
options: The domain layer, because it knows the target model
The data layer, because it knows both formats and absorbs API contract changes
The presentation layer, while rendering
A separate mapper module depending on both layers
questions.explanation: A mapper must know the DTO, so it cannot live in domain, which does not know the data layer. Placing it in data ensures that an API contract change stops at one layer boundary and the rest of the application does not feel it.

questions.text: A class takes 8 dependencies in its constructor. What does that most often signal?
options: Correct use of Dependency Injection
A Single Responsibility violation — the class does too much
The need to use a Service Locator
Missing interfaces for the dependencies
questions.explanation: The number of dependencies is often a good approximation of the number of responsibilities. Eight collaborators usually mean several independent jobs that can be split out. Replacing the constructor with a Service Locator hides the problem instead of fixing it; dependencies disappear from the signature, not from the code.

questions.text: What is “composition over inheritance”, and how is it related to SOLID?
options: It is an alternative to SOLID
Composition provides flexibility without a rigid hierarchy, supporting LSP and OCP
It applies only to languages without multiple inheritance
It requires using the Decorator pattern
questions.explanation: Inheritance creates the strongest possible coupling and easily leads to LSP violations when a subclass changes the contract. Composition — injecting a collaborator through an interface — lets behavior be swapped without changing the hierarchy. Kotlin classes are final by default for exactly this reason.

questions.text: Why should you not create a ViewModel with remember { MyViewModel() }?
options: Because remember does not work with classes
Because a ViewModel should live in a ViewModelStore; otherwise it will not survive configuration changes and will not be cleaned up
Because remember requires a key
Because a ViewModel must be a singleton
questions.explanation: remember ties the object to the composition, not to the screen lifecycle. After screen rotation a new ViewModel would be created, losing state and the MVI timeline, and viewModelScope would never be cancelled. viewModel() or koinViewModel() bind the instance to the ViewModelStore.

questions.text: What is a recomposition scope, and why does it affect performance?
options: The visibility scope of variables in a Composable
The smallest part of the UI that Compose can refresh independently
The thread on which recomposition runs
A limit on recompositions per second
questions.explanation: Compose refreshes the smallest possible scope that reads changed state. Reading state high in the tree, such as in the parent of the whole screen, expands that scope to the entire subtree. Therefore state should be read as low as possible, and lambdas can be used for deferred reads instead of passing values.

questions.text: Modifier.clickable added after Modifier.padding behaves differently than before it. Why?
options: This is a Compose bug
Modifier order matters — it determines whether padding belongs to the clickable area
clickable must always be first
padding resets earlier modifiers
questions.explanation: Modifier builds an ordered chain. padding().clickable() makes the clickable area exclude the padding, while clickable().padding() includes it. This is a common source of accessibility problems: the touch target becomes too small.

questions.text: The testing pyramid says UI tests should be the fewest. What is the main reason?
options: They are the hardest to write
They are the slowest and most brittle, and when they fail they point to the cause least precisely
They do not detect regressions
They require paid tools
questions.explanation: A UI test failing after a data-layer change does not tell you where the bug is; you must search the whole stack. A unit test points to a function. Add the time cost, minutes versus milliseconds, and brittleness from animations, timeouts, and device differences causing false alarms.

questions.text: Why is it better to use testTag than text lookup in Compose UI tests?
options: testTag is faster
Text changes with translations and copy edits, so tests break without a logic change
onNodeWithText does not work with LazyColumn
testTag is required by Espresso
questions.explanation: A test that checks logic should not depend on the exact wording of a message. Changing “Try again” to “Retry” is a copy change, not a behavior change. testTag provides a stable identifier. Exception: when the message content itself is what you are testing, asserting on text is correct.

questions.text: What is the biggest threat to the value of golden tests?
options: Large reference file size
Blindly approving new baselines, making the test always pass
Differences between Compose versions
Lack of dark mode support
questions.explanation: Clicking “update all snapshots” after every red test turns the test into a dummy. A golden test requires conscious review of the diff: is it an intended design change or a regression? Without that discipline, it is better not to have such tests than to have false confidence.

questions.text: An integration test of a ViewModel uses a real repository with a 700 ms delay. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; this is a correct integration test
The test depends on real time and should use a fake or virtual time
It should use Mockito instead of a real implementation
700 ms is too short for a stable test
questions.explanation: Real time makes tests slow and brittle, especially with timeouts on slower CI. A fake repository with controlled delay plus TestDispatcher gives full control: debounce, cancellation, and timeouts can be checked in milliseconds. Leave real implementations to E2E tests.

questions.text: A class is used as a key in HashMap. equals is overridden, but hashCode is not. What happens?
options: The compiler reports an error
map.get(key) returns null despite an equal object existing, because it goes to a different bucket
HashMap works, only slower
Objects overwrite each other
questions.explanation: HashMap first computes hashCode to choose a bucket, and only then compares with equals inside that bucket. Different hashCodes for equal objects mean lookup happens in the wrong bucket; the entry becomes unreachable even though it is physically in the map. The contract is that equal objects MUST have equal hashCode values, though not necessarily the reverse.

questions.text: An object used as a HashMap key was mutated after insertion, changing a field that affects hashCode. What is the effect?
options: The map automatically recomputes its position
The entry becomes unreachable — it is in the old bucket, while lookup searches the new one
ConcurrentModificationException is thrown
Nothing — HashMap keeps a copy of the key
questions.explanation: HashMap computes the bucket only on insertion. Mutating the key leaves the object physically in the old place while get() searches in the new one. The entry is still in the map, visible during iteration, but unreachable by key. That is why keys should be immutable; in Kotlin, use a data class with only val properties.

questions.text: What is the complexity of get() in HashMap in the pessimistic case (Java 8+)?
options: O(1) always
O(log n) — the bucket degenerates into a red-black tree
O(n) always
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Average complexity is O(1), but under collisions a bucket is a list, which used to give O(n). Since Java 8, a bucket with more than 8 entries turns into a balanced tree, so the pessimistic case is O(log n). This requires keys to be Comparable; for other types degradation can be worse.

questions.text: When is LinkedHashMap a better choice than HashMap?
options: Always — it is faster
When you need predictable iteration order or an LRU cache (accessOrder = true)
When keys are numbers
When the map is shared between threads
questions.explanation: LinkedHashMap maintains a doubly linked list of entries, giving insertion order, or access order when accessOrder=true. That second option plus removeEldestEntry is the classic LRU cache implementation in a dozen lines. The cost is extra memory for pointers.

questions.text: You are implementing an LRU cache. Which structure gives O(1) for get and put?
options: ArrayList sorted by access time
HashMap + doubly linked list, or LinkedHashMap with accessOrder
TreeMap with timestamp as key
PriorityQueue
questions.explanation: HashMap gives O(1) lookup, and a doubly linked list gives O(1) moving a node to the front and removing from the tail. A list alone would need O(n) lookup; a tree alone would be O(log n). This is a classic interview problem, and Java/Kotlin already provides the solution with LinkedHashMap.

questions.text: How does an LRU cache strategy differ from LFU?
options: LRU removes the oldest entry, LFU the largest
LRU removes the least recently used entry, LFU the least frequently used entry
LRU works in memory, LFU on disk
They are two names for the same algorithm
questions.explanation: LRU looks at TIME of last access, while LFU looks at COUNT of accesses. LFU protects constantly popular items better, but suffers from cache pollution: an item popular in the past can keep occupying space despite no current traffic. That is why variants with time windows or counter decay are used.

questions.text: A repository cache stores results indefinitely. What is the main risk?
options: A memory leak and serving stale data with no invalidation path
Slower reads
A Single Responsibility violation
No risk — cache always improves behavior
questions.explanation: A cache without eviction and invalidation policy grows without bound and eventually serves stale data. You need a size limit such as LRU, TTL, or event-based invalidation after writes. In this project, the lesson cache is intentionally indefinite because the content is immutable while the app runs.

questions.text: What is a cache stampede (thundering herd), and how can it be prevented?
options: A cache overflow caused by too-large objects
A flood of parallel requests after an entry expires; prevent it by request deduplication
A key collision in HashMap
Clearing the cache too often
questions.explanation: When a popular entry expires, all parallel requests hit the source at once. Solutions include a single flight per key, such as a per-key mutex or shared Deferred, background refresh before expiry, or randomized TTL jitter. In coroutines, a key → Deferred map fits naturally.

questions.text: When is SparseArray worth using instead of HashMap<Integer, V> on Android?
options: Always — SparseArray is faster
For small and medium collections with int keys, because it avoids autoboxing and Entry allocations
When keys are String
When the collection is shared between threads
questions.explanation: SparseArray stores two arrays, int[] and Object[], and searches with binary search, avoiding boxing and Entry objects. The memory gain is real for hundreds of entries, but lookup is O(log n) and inserting in the middle requires shifting the array. For thousands of entries, HashMap usually wins.

questions.text: What is the complexity of contains() for List and for Set?
options: Both O(1)
List O(n), hash Set O(1)
List O(log n), Set O(n)
Both O(n)
questions.explanation: A List must scan elements one by one. HashSet computes hashCode and checks one bucket. This is the most common single optimization in code: a loop with listOf(...).contains(x) inside gives O(n*m), while replacing it with a Set makes it O(n). In this project savingFavorites is a set for exactly this reason.

questions.text: How does MutableList differ from List in Kotlin at runtime?
options: List is immutable and protected from changes through other references
It is the same object — List only gives a read-only interface, not an immutability guarantee
List is copied on every assignment
List is always implemented by an array
questions.explanation: Kotlin distinguishes read-only and mutable interfaces, but underneath it is usually the same ArrayList. Casting List to MutableList, or passing the same instance elsewhere, can mutate it behind the reference holder’s back. True immutability comes from kotlinx.collections.immutable or a defensive copy.

questions.text: Which collection type is best for MVI state holding a list in Compose?
options: MutableList — it allows in-place updates
ImmutableList / PersistentList — it is stable for Compose and therefore does not force recomposition
Array — best performance
Sequence — lazy evaluation
questions.explanation: Compose treats List as unstable because it cannot know whether a mutable implementation sits underneath, so a component accepting List recomposes even with identical content. kotlinx.collections.immutable provides types marked stable. This is a real optimization for large lists.

questions.text: Why does Kotlin require a data class to have all fields in the constructor for equals/hashCode?
options: To limit the number of fields
Because generated equals/hashCode include only constructor parameters; fields in the body are ignored
Because fields in the body cannot be val
It is a compiler limitation without justification
questions.explanation: This is a common source of subtle bugs: a property declared in the class body is not included in equals, hashCode, or copy. Two objects differing only by that property will be “equal”, which breaks Set behavior, map keys, and state comparisons in MVI.

questions.text: A cache stores objects in a class field in KMP. What must you watch out for with multiple threads?
options: Nothing — Kotlin/Native freezes objects automatically
A race between reads and writes; you need atomicity or confinement to one dispatcher
Cache does not work in Kotlin/Native
You must use @Volatile on every platform
questions.explanation: After the new Kotlin/Native memory model, sharing state is allowed, but that does not make it safe. The pattern “check cache, if empty fetch and store” has a classic race: two calls can fetch data twice. Solutions include Mutex, atomic references, or a shared Deferred.

questions.text: How does Sequence differ from List in a map { }.filter { }.first() chain?
options: Sequence is always faster
List creates intermediate collections at every step; Sequence processes element by element and stops at the first hit
Sequence runs asynchronously
There is no difference; the compiler optimizes both cases
questions.explanation: On a list, every operator creates a new collection and processes all elements. Sequence is lazy: it passes a single element through the whole chain and stops when a result is found. The benefit grows with collection size and chain length, but for small collections Sequence overhead can exceed the savings.

questions.text: What is the proper way to invalidate a cache after writing data?
options: Clear the whole cache on every write
Invalidate the affected entry or update it with the written value
Set a very short TTL
Do not invalidate; data will refresh by itself
questions.explanation: Clearing everything works, but wastes valid entries and causes a wave of requests. Precise invalidation, or write-through by writing to the source and cache together, preserves consistency without losing performance. A short TTL is a workaround that does not solve stale reads immediately after a write.

questions.text: How does an inline function with reified differ from a regular generic function?
options: reified makes the call faster
reified preserves the type at runtime, so you can use is T and T::class despite type erasure
reified works only with primitive types
It is a synonym for @JvmStatic
questions.explanation: JVM generics use type erasure, so in a regular function T does not exist at runtime. inline copies the body to the call site, where the type is known; reified therefore lets you write inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T. The cost is code growth and no direct Java calls.

questions.text: How does lateinit var differ from by lazy { }?
options: lazy works only with var, lateinit with val
lateinit requires manual initialization and allows reassignment; lazy initializes once on first read
lateinit is thread-safe, lazy is not
There is no difference except syntax
questions.explanation: lateinit var is for dependency injection or initialization in onCreate; reading it before assignment throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException. by lazy is a val, computes the value on first use, and is synchronized by default with LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED. lateinit does not work with primitive types.

questions.text: What is an inline class (value class) for, and what is its main benefit?
options: Creating immutable classes
Wrapping a value without allocation overhead; the compiler inlines it to the underlying type
Speeding up serialization
Replacing enum
questions.explanation: value class UserId(val value: String) gives type safety, so you do not confuse UserId with OrderId, without creating an object at runtime because the compiler uses String directly. Boxing still happens when used as a generic type, nullable type, or when cast to an interface.

questions.text: When will Kotlin report a “Type mismatch” error for generics with out?
options: When the type is nullable
When trying to write into a covariant structure — out means it only produces values
When the generic is reified
When inheriting from an abstract class
questions.explanation: out T, covariance, lets you treat List<Dog> as List<Animal>, but only for reading; adding a Cat would break type safety. Symmetrically, in T, contravariance, only consumes. The rule is PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

questions.text: How does sealed class differ from sealed interface in Kotlin?
options: sealed interface cannot have subclasses
A class can implement multiple sealed interfaces, but inherit from only one sealed class
sealed interface does not work in when
sealed class is deprecated
questions.explanation: Inheritance is single, while interface implementation is multiple. Therefore sealed interface enables cross-cutting hierarchies; in this project UsersIntent is a sealed interface with nested Ui and Internal. Both give the compiler knowledge for exhaustive when checks.

questions.text: What does the ?: (Elvis) operator do together with return?
options: Throws an exception when the value is null
Allows an early return from a function on null — “val x = y ?: return”
Converts null to the type’s default value
It is equivalent to !!
questions.explanation: val user = users.firstOrNull { it.id == id } ?: return is an idiomatic guard clause: afterward the compiler knows user is not null through smart cast. Variants include ?: return null, ?: error("..."), and ?: throw. It is clearer than nested if (x != null).

questions.text: When will smart cast NOT work despite an if (x != null) check?
options: When x is a local val
When x is a var property of a class that another thread could change between the check and use
When x has a generic type
Smart cast always works
questions.explanation: The compiler refuses smart casts for var properties, especially from another module or with a custom getter, because it cannot guarantee the value will not change between check and use. The fix is to assign to a local val, such as val local = state.error ?: return, a common rendering-state pattern.

questions.text: How do apply and also differ, and run and let?
options: apply/run return the lambda, also/let return the receiver
apply and run operate on this, also and let on it; apply/also return the receiver, run/let return the lambda result
They all do the same thing
let works only with nullable types
questions.explanation: There are two axes: how you refer to the receiver, this versus it, and what is returned, the receiver versus the lambda result. apply configures an object with this and returns it. also performs a side effect such as logging with it and returns the object. let transforms or handles null with it and returns the result. run computes on an object with this and returns the result.

questions.text: What happens when Java code calls a Kotlin function with a default parameter?
options: Java uses the default value
Java must pass all parameters unless @JvmOverloads was added
The code does not compile
null is passed
questions.explanation: Kotlin generates one method with all parameters plus a synthetic helper method that Java does not call directly. @JvmOverloads generates overloads for parameter combinations. This matters when writing libraries consumed from Java, and it is a common interview topic.

questions.text: What is a delegated property, and what is a classic use case?
options: A property passed in the constructor
A property whose get/set delegates to another object, such as by lazy, by viewModels, or by remember
A property protected from changes
An alias for another property
questions.explanation: A delegate implements getValue/setValue, letting logic hook into property access. Standard examples are lazy, observable, vetoable, and maps. On Android, examples include by viewModels(), by remember, and by collectAsState; delegates make the code read like ordinary field access.

questions.text: What does takeIf do, and when is it idiomatic?
options: Gets the first element matching a predicate
Returns the receiver when the predicate is true, otherwise null; it composes well with Elvis
Checks the object type
It is the equivalent of filter for a single value
questions.explanation: input.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() } ?: return replaces if (input.isBlank()) return. Its sibling takeUnless reverses the condition. Overuse can be less readable than a plain if, so it is best where the result continues through a call chain.

questions.text: Why are Kotlin classes final by default?
options: For performance reasons
Because inheritance requires deliberate design — “design for inheritance or prohibit it”
Because the JVM does not support open classes
To force the use of interfaces
questions.explanation: This directly implements Effective Java advice. A class not designed for inheritance easily breaks LSP when a subclass overrides a method used internally. Kotlin requires explicit open, forcing the author to decide. Practical consequence: mocking classes requires the all-open plugin.

questions.text: What exactly does “process death” mean, and how does it differ from a configuration change?
options: They are the same phenomenon under two names
The system kills the background process; ViewModel does not survive, only SavedStateHandle/onSaveInstanceState does
Process death happens only after an app crash
After process death the app starts from the home screen
questions.explanation: A configuration change such as rotation destroys the Activity but the process stays alive, so ViewModel survives. Process death means the whole process is killed under memory pressure; the user returns to the same screen, but all in-memory objects are gone. Only data saved in Bundle, such as SavedStateHandle, survives. These are different scenarios and both need testing.

questions.text: When is SavedStateHandle worth using in MVI?
options: To store the entire screen State
To save the minimum needed to restore state, such as query or id; the rest is loaded again
Never, because ViewModel is enough
To store one-off effects
questions.explanation: Bundle size is limited and unsuitable for a user list or cache, because TransactionTooLargeException is possible. Save identifiers and inputs: query, selected category, list position. After process restoration, recreate the rest by normal data loading.

questions.text: Why is collecting a Flow in a Composable without lifecycle awareness a problem?
options: It causes a memory leak
Collection continues while the screen is in the background, wasting resources and possibly updating invisible UI
Compose does not support Flow
Flow stops emitting in the background
questions.explanation: LaunchedEffect lives as long as the composition, and the composition can remain while the app is in the background. For expensive streams such as location, sensors, or sockets, use collectAsStateWithLifecycle or repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED), which suspend collection outside the visible state.

questions.text: What is WorkManager for, and when is it NOT the right choice?
options: For immediate UI-related tasks; viewModelScope is better for those
For everything asynchronous
Only for periodic tasks
To replace coroutines
questions.explanation: WorkManager is for deferred work that must survive app closure and device restart, such as sync or upload. It has overhead: database persistence, system constraints, and delays. Fetching data for a screen belongs in viewModelScope; using WorkManager would introduce visible latency.

questions.text: What is StrictMode and what does it typically detect?
options: A compilation mode with extra warnings
A runtime tool that detects disk/network operations on the main thread and resource leaks
A screen layout debugging mode
A permissions verifier
questions.explanation: StrictMode instruments calls and reports violations: I/O on the UI thread, unclosed cursors and streams, and detected Activity instances after destruction. It is enabled in Application for debug builds. It catches problems invisible on a fast developer device but causing ANRs on weaker devices.

questions.text: An app shows an ANR. What is the time threshold for no response to input?
options: 500 ms
About 5 seconds for input events
Always 10 seconds
1 minute
questions.explanation: It is about 5 seconds for input events, around 10 seconds for a BroadcastReceiver, 20 seconds in the background, and about 20 seconds for services. ANR does not mean an exact-duration freeze; it is enough that the main thread is busy when an event arrives. Common causes are I/O on Main, long database transactions, deadlocks, and excessive GC.

questions.text: How does launchMode singleTop differ from singleTask?
options: singleTop creates a new task; singleTask does not
singleTop reuses the instance only when it is at the top of the stack; singleTask reuses it within the whole task, clearing what is above it
They are identical
singleTask does not allow multiple instances in the system
questions.explanation: singleTop calls onNewIntent if the activity is already on top, which protects against duplicates after tapping a notification twice. singleTask additionally removes activities above it. Overusing singleTask can surprisingly change Back button behavior.

questions.text: Why is passing an Activity Context to a singleton dangerous?
options: Because Context is not serializable
Because the singleton outlives the Activity and holds a reference to a destroyed screen, causing a memory leak
Because Context is not thread-safe
Because it violates Dependency Inversion
questions.explanation: Activity Context holds the entire view tree and resources. A reference from a longer-lived object prevents memory from being freed; after several rotations, several Activities remain in memory. Pass applicationContext to long-lived objects, and Activity Context only to views.

questions.text: A list in Compose scrolls with jank. Where should diagnosis start?
options: By reducing the number of items
With measurement: Layout Inspector / recomposition counts to find excessive recompositions
By adding remember to every value
By switching to RecyclerView
questions.explanation: Optimization without measurement is guessing. Android Studio tools show recomposition counts per component; typical culprits are unstable parameter types, missing key in LazyColumn, or reading frequently changing state too high in the tree. Only after diagnosis does a code change make sense.

questions.text: What does it mean that a type is “unstable” for Compose, and how can it be fixed?
options: It can throw an exception, so add try/catch
Compose cannot assume immutability, so it recomposes every time; @Immutable or immutable collections help
The type is not thread-safe
It requires remember
questions.explanation: Compose skips recomposition only for stable parameters equal to previous ones. A class with var, an interface such as List, or a type from another module without stability metrics is unstable. Fixes include @Immutable/@Stable, kotlinx.collections.immutable, or enabling strong skipping mode.

questions.text: An app starts slowly. Which metric is key, and what most often hurts it?
options: APK size
Time To Initial Display; heavy initialization in Application.onCreate hurts it
Number of methods in dex
Number of permissions
questions.explanation: Application.onCreate blocks the first render. Initialization of analytics libraries, databases, and configuration loading should be lazy or moved to App Startup/background work. Baseline Profiles also help by eliminating code interpretation cost on the first launches.

questions.text: What does a Baseline Profile do, and what effect does it have?
options: Compresses app resources
Tells ART which code paths to compile AOT before first launch
Profiles memory usage at runtime
Forces R8 full mode
questions.explanation: Without a profile, code is initially interpreted and JIT compilation happens only after repeated execution, causing jank on first launch and first screen entry. A Baseline Profile provides a list of critical methods to compile ahead of time. A typical gain is 20–30% faster startup.

questions.text: A memory leak is detected: an Activity is not freed after rotation. What is the most common cause?
options: Bitmaps are too large
A reference from a longer-lived object: static field, singleton, unregistered listener, or uncancelled coroutine
Missing System.gc() call
Too many fragments
questions.explanation: GC will not free an object reachable from a root. Typical sources are a listener registered in onCreate without unregistering, a Handler referencing Activity, a non-static inner class, or an Rx subscription without dispose. Structured concurrency and viewModelScope eliminate many of these cases.

questions.text: When is it worth passing a lambda instead of a value in Compose (deferred read)?
options: Always — lambdas are faster
When the value changes frequently: reading inside the component narrows the recomposition scope
Only for click handling
When the value is nullable
questions.explanation: Modifier.offset { IntOffset(scroll, 0) } reads scroll during the layout phase, so a change does not force recomposition; relayout is enough. Passing the value itself would recompose the whole component on every scroll frame. This is one of the most effective Compose animation optimizations.

questions.text: An MVI reducer sorts a list of 10,000 items on every intent. How can this be fixed without breaking the pattern?
options: Move sorting to the Composable
Sort once in the use case when loading, or cache the result in state instead of recalculating on every reduction
Use a mutable list and sort in place
Abandon MVI for this screen
questions.explanation: A reducer must be fast because it runs on the intent-processing thread. Sorting belongs to business rules, so the natural place is a use case, as SearchUsersUseCase does in this project. Alternatively compute once and store the result in state. A computed get() property is convenient, but it runs on every read.

questions.text: Which approach best limits the number of requests in typeahead search?
options: Increasing the request timeout
debounce + distinctUntilChanged + collectLatest
Caching all possible results
Searching only after pressing Enter
questions.explanation: debounce waits for silence, producing one request instead of one per letter; distinctUntilChanged skips repeats after deleting and typing the same character; collectLatest cancels stale requests. This trio is in UsersViewModel, and tests confirm that quickly typing three letters produces exactly one request.

questions.text: What does the “jank” metric measure, and what is the frame time budget at 60 Hz?
options: Memory usage; budget 100 MB
Frames rendered after their deadline; the budget is about 16.7 ms per frame
The number of recompositions; the budget is 60 per second
Server response time; budget 200 ms
questions.explanation: At 60 Hz, the whole cycle of composition, layout, and drawing must fit within 16.7 ms; at 120 Hz, within 8.3 ms. Exceeding that means a missed frame, which the user sees as a stutter. Measure with JankStats, Macrobenchmark, and Perfetto, not subjective smoothness.

questions.text: When should remember with a key be used instead of plain remember?
options: Always — the key speeds up lookup
When the value depends on a parameter: changing the key forces recomputation
Only in LazyColumn
When the value is expensive to compute
questions.explanation: remember(userId) { computeFor(userId) } recomputes when userId changes. Plain remember { } would keep the result for the first user and return it after the parameter changes, a very common and hard-to-spot bug because it appears only when navigating between items.

questions.text: A screen has two independent areas, each with its own loading operation. How should the state be modeled?
options: One isLoading flag for the whole screen
Separate state fields per area, or a set of identifiers for operations in progress
A separate ViewModel for each area
A list of booleans in area order
questions.explanation: A single flag collapses with a second parallel operation: the first one finishes and hides the loader of the second. In this project, the Sync screen uses Set<String> running, and Users uses savingFavorites. A set of identifiers scales to any number of operations without changing the model.

questions.text: After returning from a detail screen, the list should show updated data. How should this be solved in MVI?
options: Pass the result through a navigation argument
Keep a shared source of truth or dispatch a refresh intent on return
Refresh the list in LaunchedEffect on every recomposition
Use a global variable
questions.explanation: Passing results through navigation quickly becomes complicated. Either both screens read the same store, as in this project, or the list receives a Refresh intent on return. Refreshing on every recomposition is a bug because recomposition happens for many reasons and would trigger a storm of requests.

questions.text: How do you test that an intent did NOT trigger a side effect?
options: Check logs
Use a fake that counts calls and verify the counter did not change
It is not testable
Check whether state did not change
questions.explanation: No state change alone does not prove that no I/O happened; the operation may have run and simply not affected state. A fake with a counter gives an unambiguous assertion. This project tests the absence of a request on a repeated star tap and the request count under debounce this way.

questions.text: What happens if you call a suspend function in a coroutine finally block after cancellation?
options: It runs normally
It throws CancellationException; use withContext(NonCancellable)
It is skipped
It blocks the thread
questions.explanation: After cancellation, the coroutine is in the cancelling state and every suspend function immediately throws. If finally must perform asynchronous cleanup, such as closing a resource or saving state, wrap it in withContext(NonCancellable). Overusing this mechanism, however, creates code that cannot be stopped.

questions.text: How does Flow.stateIn differ from shareIn?
options: stateIn works only with coroutines
stateIn returns StateFlow, requiring an initial value and deduplicating; shareIn returns SharedFlow with configurable replay
shareIn is deprecated
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Both turn a cold Flow into a hot one, sharing a single subscription among receivers. stateIn is for state because it always has a value and skips duplicates; shareIn is for events. The key parameter is SharingStarted; WhileSubscribed(5000) keeps the subscription alive for 5 seconds after the last receiver leaves, surviving rotation.

questions.text: What is SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000) for, and where does that value come from?
options: It is a network request timeout
It keeps the stream alive for 5 seconds after the last subscriber leaves, surviving screen rotation without restart
It is the data refresh interval
It is the maximum lifetime of StateFlow
questions.explanation: During screen rotation the subscriber disappears and reappears shortly afterward. Without a delay, the stream would be closed and started again, causing another request. Five seconds is the Android documentation convention: long enough for a configuration change, short enough not to waste background resources.

questions.text: A use case needs data from two repositories and must combine it. Is that correct?
options: No — a use case should use exactly one repository
Yes — combining data from multiple sources is a typical business rule
No — combining belongs in the ViewModel
Yes, but only through a separate aggregator
questions.explanation: This is one of the best justifications for a use case: it encapsulates the knowledge that a given operation needs several sources. Moving that into the ViewModel would tie a business rule to the presentation layer and prevent reuse.

questions.text: An app has an offline-capable feature. Where should the “cache or network” decision live?
options: In the ViewModel, because it knows connection state
In the repository, because it knows its data sources and strategy
In the use case
In the UI layer
questions.explanation: A repository is a facade over data sources: memory, database, and network. Higher layers ask for data, not where it comes from. If the ViewModel decided the source, changing cache strategy would require presentation changes, and offline behavior would need to be implemented separately on every screen.

questions.text: You add a new method to an interface used by 10 implementations. What does that signal?
options: Normal API evolution
A possible ISP violation — perhaps the method belongs in a narrower interface implemented by only some classes
The need to use an abstract class
An LSP violation
questions.explanation: If only some implementations can provide a meaningful implementation of the new method, the rest will get empty implementations or exceptions, which leads directly to LSP violations. It signals that the interface covers more than one role. The fix is a separate narrow interface implemented by interested classes.

questions.text: A class has a method with 5 Boolean parameters. What is the main problem?
options: Too many parameters hurts performance
Flags usually mean several modes of operation in one method, violating SRP and making calls unreadable
Boolean should not be a parameter
Missing default values
questions.explanation: A call like process(true, false, true, true, false) is unreadable, and each flag usually means a separate execution path. Usually this can be split into clearly named methods or replaced with a configuration object or enum. Kotlin named arguments improve readability but do not remove excessive responsibility.

questions.text: What is CompositionLocal, and when is its use justified?
options: A cache mechanism for components
Implicitly passing values down the tree, for cross-cutting things such as theme or locale
A way to manage screen state
The equivalent of Android Context
questions.explanation: CompositionLocal fits values used everywhere and changed rarely: theme, typography, screen density. It should not pass screen state or business dependencies because it hides them from component signatures, makes tests and previews harder, and breaks explicit data flow.

questions.text: A component receives an onClick lambda that is a new instance on every recomposition. What is the effect?
options: A memory leak
The parameter changes every time, so Compose cannot skip recomposition of the subtree
Clicks stop working
No effect — lambdas are always stable
questions.explanation: Compose skips recomposition only when all parameters are equal. A new lambda instance on every pass breaks that comparison. The compiler can remember lambdas without captures, or those capturing stable values; the issue appears when unstable types are captured. The remedy is remember or a method reference.

questions.text: A test passes when run alone but fails in the suite. What is the most common cause?
options: The timeout is too short
Shared state between tests, such as static fields, singletons, or an unreset Dispatchers.Main
A bug in the test tool
Slow CI
questions.explanation: Test order is variable, so leftovers from one test break another. Common culprits are not calling stopKoin, missing Dispatchers.resetMain, a static cache, or an uncleared in-memory database. Tests must be independent; that is why this project’s Koin tests explicitly call stopKoin().

questions.text: Why use a fake repository in a test instead of a mocking library?
options: Mocks are always bad
A fake is faster, does not break on signature refactors, and reads like normal code
Mocks do not work in KMP
A fake does not require an interface
questions.explanation: Mock-based tests verify calls, so they break when order or signatures change even though behavior remains correct. A fake checks the result, not how it was achieved. A practical KMP point: most mocking libraries rely on JVM reflection and do not work in commonTest, while a fake works everywhere.

questions.text: What should a golden test verify after a design change?
options: Nothing — approve the new baselines immediately
A human reviews the diff and consciously decides whether it is an intended change
Automatic comparison with Figma
Only that the test compiles
questions.explanation: A golden test shifts responsibility to reviewing the visual diff; that is its only mechanism. Automatically approving changes turns it into a dummy that gives false confidence. Reference files therefore belong in the repository and go through code review like any other change.

questions.text: You want to use a JVM-only library in commonMain. What are your options?
options: Add it to commonMain; Gradle will handle it
Define an interface in commonMain and provide per-platform implementations, using expect/actual or DI
Copy the library code into the project
Drop iOS support
questions.explanation: commonMain compiles for all targets, so a JVM-only dependency breaks the Kotlin/Native build. The standard solution is an abstraction in commonMain, a JVM implementation in androidMain, and a native implementation in iosMain. First check whether a multiplatform equivalent exists, such as ktor, okio, or kotlinx-*.

questions.text: Why is it worth limiting the public API of the shared KMP module exposed to iOS?
options: Because it reduces framework size and simplifies interop; fewer types cross through Objective-C
Because Swift does not support more than 100 classes
Because public API is slower
Because iOS requires an explicit export list
questions.explanation: Every public type ends up in the Objective-C header, increasing framework size and compile time. The narrower the API, the fewer Kotlin peculiarities, such as sealed types, generics, and default values, leak into Swift in inconvenient forms. Expose a facade and mark the rest internal.

questions.text: Rx code runs on the wrong thread despite subscribeOn(Schedulers.io()). What is a possible cause?
options: subscribeOn works only with Flowable
There is more than one subscribeOn in the chain, and only the first one counts
observeOn is missing
Schedulers.io() does not exist
questions.explanation: subscribeOn affects the source subscription, so later calls in the chain are ignored. This is a common bug when composing streams from several layers, each adding its own subscribeOn. observeOn is different: it applies from its position downward and can be used multiple times.

questions.text: What is backpressure, and why does Flow not need a separate type like Flowable?
options: It is a limit on the number of subscribers
It is when a producer emits faster than the consumer can process; Flow solves it by suspending the emitter
It is an error retry mechanism
It is a Channel buffer size limit
questions.explanation: In Rx, the consumer must explicitly request n items, and Observable without this mechanism can run into OutOfMemoryError. Flow uses suspension: emit() simply waits until the consumer is ready. Backpressure is therefore built into the model, while buffer and conflate intentionally relax it.

questions.text: You need a platform abstraction in commonMain. What is the decisive question when choosing between expect/actual and an interface plus DI?
options: Which one compiles faster
Whether anything in it is worth substituting in a test
Whether the code lives in the domain or the data layer
Whether iOS supports the API at all
questions.explanation: An actual cannot be replaced: there is exactly one per target, picked by the compiler. If a test would ever want to control the behaviour — return a value, simulate a failure — the abstraction must be an interface. Compile time and layer placement are secondary; substitutability is what decides.

questions.text: What is the practical consequence of implementing a persistent store as expect/actual instead of an interface?
options: It stops working in Kotlin/Native
Any test touching that path pulls in the real platform implementation, so it cannot run on the JVM
The code becomes slower because of dynamic dispatch
Nothing — the two approaches are equivalent
questions.explanation: An actual is resolved by the compiler, so there is no seam to substitute. A JVM test would need a real SharedPreferences and therefore an emulator or Robolectric. With an interface the same test runs in milliseconds against an in-memory fake, which is exactly why KeyValueStore is a port in this project.

questions.text: Which of these is the best candidate for expect/actual rather than a port?
options: Reading the saved user session
Setting the status bar icon tone
Checking whether the device is online
Generating a unique identifier
questions.explanation: Setting the icon tone is a one-way side effect: no state, no branching, no return value, and on iOS it is a no-op. A fake could only assert that the call happened, which tests the mock. The other three all hold state or make a decision that a test needs to control, so they belong behind an interface.

questions.text: Why is this a poor use of expect/actual?
options: expect functions cannot return Long
Time becomes uncontrollable in tests — expiry could only be verified by waiting for it
It will not compile for Kotlin/Native
currentTimeMillis is already available in the standard library
questions.explanation: The problem is testability, not syntax. With the clock hidden behind an actual, a test cannot pretend that time has passed, so the only way to reach the expired branch is to wait for it. A `fun interface Clock` injected into the validator makes the same logic testable in microseconds. Anything that is a decision, not a raw platform call, belongs behind an interface.
questions.code:
expect fun currentTimeMillis(): Long

fun isTokenExpired(expiry: Long) = currentTimeMillis() > expiry

questions.text: How does a platform dependency passed as a parameter compare with expect/actual and DI?
options: It is a worse variant of DI, because it exposes an implementation detail
It keeps the dependency visible in the signature, lets previews use a default and keeps Context out of shared code
It only works for Compose functions
It prevents the use of Koin
questions.explanation: `App(platformModule: Module = previewPlatformModule())` states the dependency in the signature instead of hiding it in a global. Android passes SharedPreferences, iOS passes NSUserDefaults, and previews fall back to an in-memory default with no configuration. Visibility in a signature is a feature: the reader sees what the function needs.

questions.text: A tutorial tells you to call freeze() before sharing state between threads in Kotlin/Native. How should you read that advice today?
options: Correct — freezing is still required for shared state
Obsolete — the new memory model removed freezing in Kotlin 1.7.20
Correct, but only for objects captured by coroutines
Correct only on iOS, not on macOS
questions.explanation: The old model required freeze() and threw InvalidMutabilityException on mutation of a frozen object, which made coroutines painful and drove teams away from KMP. Since 1.7.20 state is shared between threads as on the JVM. Advice about freeze(), @ThreadLocal and AtomicReference predates that change — always check the date on KMP material.

questions.text: Your team shares the domain and data layers but keeps SwiftUI on iOS. How should this be judged?
options: A half-measure — the point of KMP is sharing the UI as well
A legitimate architecture that captures most of the benefit, since the risky complexity lives in the logic
Impossible — Compose Multiplatform is required for KMP
Reasonable only for small apps
questions.explanation: The payoff from sharing falls as you move outward: domain and data hold the complexity worth writing once, while the UI is where platform conventions matter most. Keeping native UI is a common and deliberate choice. It does impose one constraint: the shared layers must not depend on Compose, which is exactly why the domain stays plain Kotlin.

questions.text: You export a Kotlin sealed interface to iOS. What does a Swift developer actually get?
options: A Swift enum with associated values and exhaustive matching
A protocol with implementing classes, and switch still needs a default branch
A struct holding a type discriminator
Nothing — sealed types are not exported
questions.explanation: Interop goes through Objective-C, which has no notion of sealed types, so exhaustiveness is lost and the compiler stops helping. It is a real cost when the shared API models state as a sealed hierarchy. SKIE generates native Swift enums on top, restoring exhaustive matching — worth adopting before hand-writing wrappers.

questions.text: Why keep the API exported from a shared module narrow?
options: Kotlin/Native limits the number of exported classes
Every public type lands in the Objective-C header, inflating framework size and compile time, and leaking Kotlin quirks into Swift
Public declarations are slower to call
iOS requires an explicit export list
questions.explanation: The generated header grows with every public declaration, and each one exposes Kotlin constructs — sealed types, generics, default arguments — in whatever awkward shape Objective-C allows. A narrow facade with the rest marked internal keeps both the framework and the Swift-side experience manageable.

questions.text: Which claim about KMP is FALSE?
options: Build times grow, because each target compiles separately
A bug in shared code now reaches both apps at once
Sharing code removes differences in permissions and background execution
A JVM-only dependency cannot be used from commonMain
questions.explanation: Platform behaviour is not unified by sharing code: permissions, background limits and lifecycles still differ and still need platform handling. The other three are genuine trade-offs — and the shared-bug one is an argument for more tests, not fewer, since a single defect now ships twice.

questions.text: You are modelling the blocks of a lesson: a paragraph carries text, a table carries headers and rows, an exercise carries a number and text. enum or sealed?
options: enum, with the data held in a Map on the side
A plain class hierarchy with an open base class
enum, with a nullable field for every variant
sealed, because the data differs from case to case
questions.explanation: An enum forces every entry into the same shape, so the variants would collapse into one class with a nullable field per case — the classic bag of optionals, where invalid combinations become representable and every reader guesses which fields are set. A sealed hierarchy gives each case exactly the data it needs and keeps `when` exhaustive. An open class would additionally lose exhaustiveness.

questions.text: A bottom bar has to render every tab. Each tab has a label and an icon. Which construct, and what settles it?
options: enum, because entries share a shape and `entries` iterates them for free
sealed, because tabs may gain different data later
sealed, because it interops better with Swift
Either — the choice makes no practical difference
questions.explanation: All tabs have identical shape, so an enum fits, and `Tab.entries` is what settles it: a sealed hierarchy has no built-in way to enumerate its subtypes, so the bar would need a hand-maintained list that someone eventually forgets to update. The Swift claim is backwards — an enum maps to a real Swift enum, while sealed becomes a protocol and loses exhaustiveness.

questions.text: A code review adds `else -> throw IllegalStateException()` to a `when` over a sealed interface, to “be safe”. What is the effect?
options: It is safer — unexpected subtypes now fail loudly
It removes the compiler's completeness check, so a new subtype becomes a runtime failure instead of a build error
No effect — the compiler ignores an unreachable else
It only affects code coverage numbers
questions.explanation: Without `else` the compiler lists every place that has to handle a new subtype, turning the addition into a mechanical to-do list. With `else` the code compiles happily and fails when a user hits that path. The branch trades a build error for a production incident — the opposite of safe, despite how it reads.

questions.text: Why should an enum's `ordinal` never be persisted or sent over the wire?
options: It is a private implementation detail and will not compile
It is not available in Kotlin/Native
Reordering entries silently changes it, so stored data starts pointing at a different constant
It is not stable across Kotlin versions
questions.explanation: `ordinal` is simply the declaration index, so inserting an entry in the middle shifts everything after it. Nothing fails at compile time and nothing throws at runtime — previously stored values quietly mean something else. `name` is stable against reordering, which is why the preferences in this project store `ThemeMode.Dark` rather than an index.

questions.text: You need a Result type carrying either a value of type T or an error. Which construct can express this at all?
options: enum class, with a generic parameter
Either — both support generics
Neither — it requires an open class
sealed, because enums cannot be generic
questions.explanation: Enums cannot declare type parameters: entries are singletons created at class-initialisation time, and a generic singleton has no single type to be. A sealed hierarchy has no such limit, so `sealed interface Result<out T>` with `Success<T>` and `Failure` is the standard shape. This is one of the few places where the choice is forced rather than a matter of taste.

questions.text: What does `data object` add over a plain `object` inside a sealed hierarchy?
options: It permits multiple instances
It makes the object serializable automatically
It reduces memory usage
It generates a readable toString() and a proper equals(), which debug output and logs depend on
questions.explanation: A plain object inherits the default toString(), so it prints as `RefreshClicked@4f3a2b1c` — useless in a log or on an intent timeline. `data object` generates the class name instead, and an equals() based on identity rather than the default reference check. Both objects remain singletons; only the generated members differ.

questions.text: Serializing a sealed hierarchy to JSON requires more setup than an enum. Why?
options: Each subtype has a different shape, so the JSON needs a discriminator to say which one it is
Sealed types have no stable name to serialize
Because sealed subtypes may live in other modules
Sealed types are not supported by kotlinx.serialization
questions.explanation: An enum serialises to its name and that is the whole story — `"category": "mvi"` is unambiguous. A sealed hierarchy carries different fields per subtype, so the reader needs an extra field, configured here as `classDiscriminator = "type"` with `@SerialName` on each subtype. That asymmetry is a genuine argument for an enum whenever the wire format is simple.

questions.text: Why does this project use `sealed interface` almost everywhere and `sealed class` only for UserSyncException?
options: Interfaces can hold state, classes cannot
sealed class is deprecated
Interfaces perform better
A class can implement several interfaces but extend only one class, and UserSyncException must extend Exception
questions.explanation: Single inheritance is the constraint. `sealed interface` lets a type participate in several hierarchies, which is what makes nesting like `Ui : UsersIntent` work. `UserSyncException` has no such freedom: it must extend `Exception` to be throwable, so the sealed hierarchy has to be a class. Neither performance nor deprecation plays any part.
